utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As you know, this is not going to be a full week. In principle, starting on Wednesday, I don't actually know whether the plenary is going to last for two or three days, but there is going to be a shortened week. That's how it is. First of all, does everybody hear me? I suppose everybody does. I would like to say good afternoon to the interpreters and to the attorneys both from the Prosecution and the Defence. Does the Defence hear me? General Blaskic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that the Prosecutor would now exercise his right of reply in the continued examination of Colonel Morsink, and it was Mr. Harmon who was doing it (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Lieutenant-Colonel. Did you have a nice weekend? Did you rest up -- or I shouldn't say weekend in French, I should say fin de semaine, weekend. If you did, we can continue now, not the examination-in-chief or the cross-examination, but the right of reply, since you were called in by the Prosecution, Mr. Harmon is going to ask you some questions. I see that Mr. Dubuisson is looking at me. I must have made an error. Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, and counsel. Could I have Exhibit 296 placed on the ELMO and could I also have Exhibit 414 given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, first I'd like to return to the issue of HVO, HDZ propaganda that was directed to the Croats living in the Zenica area, and your investigation into it as well as your findings that the claims about atrocities and mass destruction of Croat homes of the Muslims were exaggerated and false. In respect of your investigation into the Croat villages and the destruction that related to those villages, you were asked by Mr. Hayman the following questions, and I'm referring to the English translation of the unofficial transcript, I'm reading from page 9951, lines 5 through 7 and lines 11 through 14: You were asked the following questions. Question: You have told us that the church at Guca Gora was not touched in the course of that action; is that correct? And your answer was: That's correct. I visited that church myself after the fighting passed from the north across Guca Gora in a southern direction. The next question you were asked was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next question you were asked was: And that neighbouring Croat communities, no wanton destruction or attack on civilian structures by the BiH army, or was there such conduct in the Guca Gora region generally? And you answered that neither you nor your colleagues saw extensive damage in those Croat communities in and around Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember that line of questioning, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I remember that line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next thing; Mr. Hayman directed your attention to Exhibit 296 which is located to your right on the ELMO, and he then referred you to a paragraph, paragraph 1 of Prosecutor's Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you speak a little more slowly, please, Mr. Harmon, for the sake of the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I apologise. And apologies to the interpreters as well. You were next directed, Mr. Morsink, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 414, first paragraph, Mr. Hayman read to you the following sentence: "UNPROFOR further report the Croat village of Dolac as deserted and over 100 houses burnt."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I remember that question as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you were also asked whether that very same day, which was the 8th of June, it was reported by UNPROFOR that in the village of Dolac these 100 houses had been burnt. Now, Colonel Morsink, would you turn to Prosecutor's Exhibit 296, and using the pointer, could you point to the village of Dolac. It's in Prosecutor's Exhibit 296.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: (indicated).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now is that the Dolac that is referred to in paragraph 1 of Prosecutor's Exhibit 414, that is, is that the Dolac where UNPROFOR reported that over 100 houses were burnt?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It's not Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the village of Dolac, where over 100 houses were reported burning, even located in the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, again, would you return to Prosecutor's Exhibit 414, which is -- I refer to paragraph number 1. Let me return to the complete -- let me read the complete sentence then that was read to you in part by

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR further report the Croat village of Dolac (YJ1399) as deserted and over 100 houses burnt." Which municipality, Colonel Morsink, is Dolac with the coordinates YJ1399 located?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: According to the grid, Dolac is located in the vicinity of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if I could have the following exhibit marked and placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 429.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, would you kindly explain to the Judges what is represented in Prosecutor's Exhibit 429?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Travnik, you can see two Dolacs that we appreciated as being one small village, one is called Dolac and the other one is called Dolac Na Lasvi, it's something like near the Lasva River. The correct way is to read the grid is first find the two letters, they are placed here in this part, that means 100 kilometre square. In the UTM system. Then you take the vertical, 13, and then the horizontal, that's 99, so the correct grid of this Dolac should be YJ1399.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is the area where it was reported 100 Croat houses burning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you turn to the other coordinates located on Prosecutor's Exhibit 429 and explain to the Judges those coordinates?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: First we find the two letters again, that's YK, then we find the vertical, that is 27, and horizontal, that's 01, so this Dolac would be YK2710 (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And YK2701 is the Dolac that's referred to in Prosecutor's Exhibit 296; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, that's the same Dolac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges, please, Colonel Morsink, what was happening on the 8th of June in and around the Dolac that is marked with the coordinates YJ1399?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: According to our knowledge at that time, there was major fighting going on in the outskirts of Travnik, so that's exactly this Dolac area here, the HVO used to control a major checkpoint on the main road from Vitez to Travnik, and the fighting was about this checkpoint and about the frontlines moving in the town of Dolac, so there was a major fight going on in Dolac itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the Dolac where the 100 houses were reported burning was a major front-line battle ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, it was a real battle ground at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, in fact, later when Dolac with coordinates YJ1399 was visited by ECMM, they assessed, in fact, that approximately 15 to 20 houses had been burnt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, so that's far less than the 100 first reported by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did they also make an assessment on the Catholic church that was in Dolac at coordinates YJ1399?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. The church is even on the map. This church was hit by a single mortar round and, because of that mortar impact, damaged, the roof was damaged and part of the interior was damaged. There was no sign of fighting directly targeted on this church.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that was assessed to be not intentional damage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That was assessed by us as not intentionally damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Therefore, Colonel Morsink, in respect of ECMM's investigation into the events in and around Guca Gora on the 8th of June, 1993, you stand by your previous testimony and by ambassador Thebault's conclusion that the allegations of atrocities or ethnic cleansing made by the Bosnian Croats are intentionally exaggerated, when not completely false?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, I still stand by that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would move to admit Prosecutor's Exhibit 429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection? No discussion? All right. Then this exhibit will be admitted under the number that was assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different subject now, please, Colonel Morsink. You were asked questions about Prosecutor's Exhibit 418 which is a letter from Mate Boban to General Morillon which is dated the 22nd of June, 1993, in which Mate Boban alleges that the Croatian people of Central Bosnia were on the verge of being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What number is that, please? Oh, yes, I have it here, yes, yes, I have it. 418; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In Prosecutor's Exhibit 418, Mate Boban says, "The Croatian people of Central Bosnia are on the verge of extinction and being expelled from areas where they have lived for over 13 centuries. UNPROFOR and yourself have witnessed the barbaric Muslim devastation and desecration of sacred Catholic objects of our people, and it goes on referring to Guca Gora and other locations. Now, could you again refer to Prosecutor's Exhibit 414, specifically the first page of that document, and the report authored by Ambassador Thebault. Ambassador Thebault in Prosecutor's Exhibit 414 referred to a public claim by Mate Boban that was issued prior to the 8th of June, 1993, wherein Mate Boban appealed to the International Community to save the Croats from extinction.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what Mr. Thebault says in his special report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is the tone of the report from Ambassador Thebault of what Mate Boban had to say and the tone of what Mate Boban had to say in Prosecutor's Exhibit 418 consistent with the tone that you read in then Colonel Blaskic's Call to Help which was dated the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: All these letters fit into the same structure, same attempts to -- according to my opinion, to mislead their own people and to mislead the international opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, I'd like to turn now to Defence Exhibit 145, and if that could be given to the witness? Now, this exhibit, Colonel Morsink, is a council of Europe 6th information report on war damage to the cultural war damage to Bosnia and Herzegovina presented by the committee on culture and education, and it's a report on a fact-finding mission from the 30th of May to the 22nd of June, 1994, by Dr. Colin Kaiser. In your cross-examination, Counsel read a paragraph from this document to you. The paragraph he read is as follows: "Guca Gora. The civil and military BiH authorities in Travnik permitted the consultant to visit this site. The village, which contained many traditional farmhouses and buildings, was taken from the HVO, perhaps by Mujahedin soldiers, and it was ethnically cleansed of Croats with a lot of burning. Two weeks later, the ABiH occupied the Franciscan monastery which it still occupies." Now, let me -- have you had a chance to review this document, Defence Exhibit 145?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: You showed it to me later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you read the paragraph that followed that particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, that following paragraph indicates, does it not, that while Dr. Kaiser, the consultant who authored this report, could not visit the interior of the church and the monastery buildings, he could see that the exterior and grounds had suffered only insignificant damage. Is that what he reports?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does he also say that -- further on: "Other items of value (paintings, liturgical items, et cetera), were evacuated to Travnik where they are safeguarded by the local authorities." Does he say that as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you visited this particular site, this Franciscan monastery, many times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you go into the interior of this monastery?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I went in twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the two times that you went in, which was prior to Dr. Kaiser's visit, was the interior side of the monastery damaged in any way?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, it was undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And similarly was the exterior of the monastery damaged or undamaged when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It was undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, further down in Defence Exhibit 145, I'd like to read a paragraph to you. It starts with the word "Kruscica: Unfinished new mosque hit in facade perhaps by recoilless canon (HVO). Roof was also damaged but fixed. An example of deliberate mosque shooting since the houses in this largely traditional village seemed to have suffered little from shelling." Now, Colonel Morsink, were you aware of this attack that is referred to in Dr. Kaiser's report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the same attack as I addressed to Mario Cerkez when I was there in that area. I think it was the beginning of May when I was asked -- when I asked Mario Cerkez why HVO soldiers were shooting with anti-tank rockets at the mosque in Kruscica. I believe it was the same mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was Mario Cerkez' reply to you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: His answer, interpreted by my interpreter, was, "I could ask the other side the same thing."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he appear to be concerned about an allegation made by you that the mosque in Kruscica had been deliberately targeted?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different subject in the cross-examination. You were asked some questions about your attempts to visit the village of Gomionica on the 27th of April, 1993, and not being able to enter the village to inspect it. Based, according to a soldier at the roadblock, on the orders of Ivica Rajic. Was Ivica Rajic the HVO Brigade commander in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He was during a certain period. They told me that later on he was killed at the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was Ivica's Rajic's superior officer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think Mr. Blaskic was his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to return again to the subject of Kruscica, and specifically your testimony about your efforts to provide Kruscica with humanitarian aid. Your testimony on direct examination was that you attempted to deliver humanitarian aid to Kruscica for approximately five weeks, and that the excuse that was given to you by HVO officials was that the road to Kruscica was being blocked by angry civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you further testified that you and -- I'm sorry, that you fully informed the HVO, including deputy commander Nakic, of your efforts to resupply Kruscica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. On more than one occasion and to different HVO representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that approximately five weeks later, you succeeded in entering into Kruscica, but this time by an alternate parallel road that was controlled by the HVO and of which you were unaware; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question is this: Was this alternate parallel road the one that had been blocked by angry civilians or was this a completely different road?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It was a completely different road. The main road was blocked by angry civilians, and this appeared to be another parallel road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, could this alternate parallel road have been opened by the HVO at any time during the five weeks preceding your actual delivery of aid on the 21st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure it could have been opened at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Because during that period of five weeks, the front-line didn't seem to move, there was no major fighting going on in the outskirts of Kruscica or Vitez, so I think the situation in the beginning of the five-week period was exactly the same as at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you testified briefly about the Busovaca Joint Commission, and you said that that was -- that that commission had been created in part because of serious violations of international humanitarian law that had occurred in Busovaca in January of 1993, violations which in part were committed by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's what I was told by my colleague monitors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if a commander is aware that his subordinates have a propensity toward committing these kind of serious violations of humanitarian law and if the commander later plans and organises a large-scale and systematic operation directed at Muslim villages in the same community and adjacent communities, what should the commander do, in your opinion, to ensure that these same violations of international humanitarian law do not re-occur?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope, Mr. President. If counsel wants to repeat his direct, so be it. If so, it should be with the consent of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, either reformulate the question or it is true that you're somewhat outside the scope of the cross-examination. You're redoing an examination-in-chief here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the subject of Djuti, Colonel Morsink. You testified that Djuti had been described to you as an uncontrolled element of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You further testified that you met Djuti once in the presence of deputy commander Nakic and brigade commander Leotar. My question is; where did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That meeting took place at the headquarters of Mr. Leotar, the Brigade commander, and I believe it was in a small village called Bilici north-west of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that was an HVO headquarters, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, it was in the Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would Djuti have been arrested by HVO when you saw him in the headquarters on the 2nd of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. It was HVO controlled area. There were a lot of guards in these headquarters, so he could easily have been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the subject of the humanitarian aid that was confiscated in Busovaca. You testified that on the 2nd of July, 1993, you met with Pakco (phoen) Ljubesic who was the police chief. You asked for the release of aid, and Mr. Ljubesic told you that he first had to ask permission from his superiors in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were then asked to return the following day, and you did, and, in fact, on the following day you testified that you met an HVO brigade commander by the name of Grubesic, and he told you that based on the orders from the HVO headquarters in Vitez, that the seized humanitarian aid would be released if the threat from Zenica was eliminated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. It was linked to the roadblock just put there that very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, is the decision of the HVO not to release the humanitarian aid until the military threat from Zenica was removed consistent with Colonel Blaskic having tactical control over the military police in his theatre of operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Beyond the scope again, Mr. President, and I object to the way Counsel is leading the witness. Admittedly, some leading has to occur on redirect, but the leading here is beyond anything I think I've ever seen in a court of law on either direct or redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't believe the examination is beyond the scope in this particular ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to reformulate your question, Mr. Harmon, so as not to give Mr. Hayman the impression that this is the first court he's ever been in when his opponent is going somewhat outside the scope of the initial examination. Try to reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, when you returned on the 3rd of July and you were told by the HVO brigade commander that there was a connection between the release of humanitarian aid and the removal of a threat from Zenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. For the time being, we are within the scope of the cross-examination, Mr. Hayman. That's what -- for the time being, this is the scope of the examination. Is that not so, Mr. Hayman? All right. Continue now, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, then, in your view, was that consistent with Colonel Blaskic having tactical control over military police in his area of operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, here the problem is new --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. He hasn't completed with his question. I'm trying to see whether your objection is valid. At least let me listen to the question all the way to the end. I specifically tried to set up kind of a split here in the middle for the first part of the sentence, the question is within the scope of the cross-examination, at least let me hear the end of the question. Mr. Harmon, please start again. We are within the scope of the cross-examination when it has to do with knowing whether we're speaking about humanitarian aid which was interrupted. Mr. Harmon, will you continue with your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. President, is a question that was touched upon by Counsel. That is the tactical control of a commander in an area of operations, and my question to Colonel Morsink is: Was the fact that the police chief told you he had to get permission from Busovaca -- I'm sorry, from Mostar, and then you returned the following day when you were told by a military commander, a brigade commander, that there was a connection, that you couldn't get back the aid until a threat, a military threat from Zenica, was removed, suggests, does it not, that the permission received by the police chief was overridden as a tactical matter by the commander in the operations zone. Is that how you would interpret that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. I think the police matter was overruled by the military commander in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I state my objection now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel, is it normal that an operation zone commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I said that the question was proper. If you want to object to something else, about something else ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just want to state for the record why I object, and it is because new opinions of an expert nature are being elicited from the witness on redirect. We will never have the opportunity to cross-examine the witness on those new opinions, and I think that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, we are being very attentive. On various occasions I have had the opportunity to say that the right of rebuttal must be part of the scope of the cross-examination and that the rule that the cross-examination must be part of the examination-in-chief is not a mathematical formula. You understand that when you yourself bring in your witnesses. Things are not absolutely precise. Each time the judge has to hear the objections and to decide in respect of that objection whether there is a truth here that has to be got at. Of course, sometimes I myself have to consult with my colleagues, but it does seem to me that in this particular case, this is a field -- a scope which was covered by your own cross-examination. All of this is now in the transcript in order to accommodate your wishes, and this has not, however, changed the position of the Judges. Mr. Harmon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it normal that an operation zone commander would have tactical control over units in his area, all units in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think it's necessary that he has tactical control over all units in his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence also showed you a film and asked you to identify an individual, and the film was taken at a location known as "the bungalow" the night before the attack on the village of Ahmici which occurred on the 16th of April, 1993. Based on your knowledge of military structures, would a military police unit that is involved in a well-organised and coordinated attack be outside the tactical control of the operation zone commander?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think that's impossible to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges why?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, if a commander has to organise a military operation in his area of responsibility, then he has to control all his elements, he has to be in tactical command over all his elements. There cannot be any exception, with units doing other operations on somebody else's initiative, so it should be under the command of one person and one person only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions of this witness. I have concluded my redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Very well, Lieutenant-Colonel. The Judges will ask you some questions themselves or for some additional clarifications which they would like to have from you. First I turn to Judge Riad. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have a certain number of questions to ask you if you are in a position to enlighten me, enlighten us, although definitely you have been very clear, and I do not mean by that that you were not clear, but there is always room for more clarification. I'll start from the beginning, although it goes back in time. I hope I haven't forgotten. You spoke of a certain Mr. Pedersen who asked for an investigation -- who once asked for an investigation, I think that was after the truck bomb in Vitez, and Cerkez accepted the investigation idea but nothing has been done. Can you tell me what is Cerkez in relationship to General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Cerkez, Mario Cerkez, was a Brigade commander of the HVO brigade in Vitez, located in Vitez with its headquarters in Vitez, and he was subordinate to Mr. Blaskic being the commander of the operational zone middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he represented General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you think the investigation would be carried out by Mr. Cerkez in the name of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: According to our marshal law, the Brigade commander is responsible for his own area of operations, in this case being the town or the vicinity of Vitez, so I think it would be appropriate if Mr. Mario Cerkez had done the investigation. If he didn't have any means to do so, then he could ask for support from his superior. He would at least have reported to his superior that he had done the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This leads me to another question. Suppose he did not report to his superior. Was the incident so remote from General Blaskic that he would not have taken knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think this truck bomb was so severe that we could hear it from 5 kilometres distance and the location of the truck bomb was only 500 metres away from the headquarters of Mr. Blaskic, so he must have heard it, or at least his soldiers in his headquarters must have heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Even if Mr. Cerkez did not report it to him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. This was such a huge explosion. Everybody in Vitez knew about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you were speaking always of the truck bomb in Vitez. You mentioned that the evacuation took place, there were 200 wounded or something like that, and Colonel Stewart was very angry because the HVO did not help the wounded and only the British battalion did the evacuation. Was this a normal method not to help the wounded everywhere or -- I mean, was the HVO in the habit of not participating in saving the civilians?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the only clear occasion where HVO, according to my knowledge, failed to help. I don't know whether it happened the same thing in other occasions. But I think they were organised and capable of helping because they -- the civil and military government in Vitez, they were the ones who ruled the local Red Cross organisation, who ruled the other organisations like the fire brigade, and they were the ones who had the trucks, the ambulances. So if anybody could have helped, then they could have, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they never did?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: They never did, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm just following your testimony, so perhaps it's not related. You also mentioned that at the roadblocks, you had been refused access and even threatened at the HVO roadblocks. Now, was there any animosity between your groups and the HVO? Was there any ill-feelings? Why would they act like that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Sometimes there was animosity because they accused the UNHCR of bringing ammunition to the other side. They sometimes accused UNPROFOR of being partial, and they even sometimes accused us of not doing what we had promised, like freeing prisoners or removing threats from any direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And there was no other reason, you think? There was no other reason for this -- for stopping you from access?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, the reason they told us for the human roadblock was that a woman was killed in her back yard and she was shot twice. The first time she was hit, her child tried to evacuate her from the back yard into the house, and when the child was with her, she was hit again and killed in that accident, and that was such -- it was a pitiful accident, everybody could feel that, and we felt the same way, and they told us that that was the reason why angry civilians blocked that road, because of this single accident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned also that Mario Kordic threatened once to burn Kruscica totally, I think it was in case of attack?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That was Mario Cerkez, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, Mario Cerkez, yes. Why was that exactly? Why did he threaten to burn the city?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He mentioned this threat during a meeting of the local commission Vitez. During this meeting, the problem of Kruscica was raised again, and Mario Cerkez claimed that the army of BiH was bringing in new troops through the mountains on a small trail, goat trail, so not a normally-used road, and because of these fresh troops, they thought that the army of BiH were planning an attack coming from Kruscica in the direction of Vitez, I think. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was Kruscica a military centre?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: There was a part of a Muslim brigade in Kruscica. I'm not sure, I think a battalion or one and a half battalions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Is it normal in wartime that if there is a battalion in a city, you burn the whole city?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, that's not normal because there were more than 4.000 civilians living in the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it part of the system of the HVO to burn a city if there is any weapons in it or that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they claimed that that was the reason why they burned down a village, like in Rotilj, the seven houses. But we had seen examples of burned-down villages already in the area, so that's the reason why we took this threat seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it's not one of the methods of war?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Not according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- to burn cities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Not according to our laws, and I think everybody should obey those laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you think Cerkez was supposed to speak in the name of General Blaskic or his own name? Was he freelance?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He could have spoken in his own name, but then he was the known brigade commander, known by everybody. We were in theatre already for a few weeks then. And he introduced himself more than once as the brigade commander. He commanded his troops, and he was in function when he said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Speaking of commander, you mentioned very categorically that the command structure of the HVO in middle Bosnia was well-structured and with good communication and good execution of orders and control of telephone lines and so on. Now, speaking of commanders, who was considered the commander, when you speak of the command structure being respected?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic was considered to be the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez was his subordinate, so Mr. Blaskic was the supreme commander in the area, and Mr. Cerkez was one of the brigade commanders. There were more brigade commanders, of course, I think he had five or six brigades in the area of -- from Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, to Kiseljak, and then if you -- there were even more brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But also all subordinate to the big commander?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: All subordinate to the big commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And as you said, the command structure was perfect?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, "perfect" might be a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Militarily speaking, it was well organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a double policy, a double operation, done by the military side and the political side at the same time. This double operation was, first, the ethnic cleansing of Muslims through fear, killing, and burning; the other policy was to frighten the Croat minorities in the other places so that they might immigrate to the areas that had been ethnically cleansed. Would this be the policy of the military, or a political policy? What would be the roles-- how would you distribute the roles of the military and the political command in it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think the military part would set the preconditions for it, and the part of pulling Croats from outside into the region would have been probably registered by the politicians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So who do you think would be the responsible -- the ultimate responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's hard to say. I'm not fully familiar with the top political structure in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you mentioned the political here. Would the burning of, for instance, Vitez or that sort of thing, be attributed to the political commander?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, to the military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The military commander. Now, you mentioned that Merdan -- he was a general? What was he?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: He was a deputy commander of the third corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He told you several times that the 7th Muslim brigade was not under his control, and then by the end of May it became under his control, and he informs you. Now, did you receive any similar information from the HVO that certain battalions -- or certain brigades were not under the control of the commander the way Merdan told you about his 7th brigade?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The HVO made several suggestions like that, but they were always undefined, uncontrolled elements, so no names of brigades or battalions, just as a common word "uncontrolled units" or "uncontrolled elements."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When would they make such affirmations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: When there were any allegations on war crimes during one of the meetings, they would blame the uncontrolled elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As a defence?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: As a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But what Merdan told you was not a defence? Was it a defence too?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe it was a defence in the beginning, but I have think he was -- he wasn't very happy about this 7th Muslim brigade and he showed us that he tried to put this brigade under his control and he finally succeeded, as he told us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I still have another question. You mentioned there was an exhibit, I think D151, the order of General Blaskic to stop certain violations, and the order was given to a unit under his authority. Now, such an order was supposed to be followed up by investigation or punishment. Were you informed about the result of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I was never informed of any results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the order stopped at that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I'm not sure, of course, but we were not informed about any investigations or results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that even after there was an agreement, even after the agreement in Stranje by the joint military commission, digging trenches continued. Is that -- is did I understand it right or did it stop?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, that is correct, you understand it right. The allegations on people being forced to dig trenches went on, so I didn't see any examples myself after that, but the allegations went on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned -- this is my last question, perhaps -- that Nakic was a representative of General Blaskic to the joint operational command, ordered unconditional cease-fire once but the local HVO commander did not obey. Were there any INCIDENTS where direct orders from Colonel Blaskic were not obeyed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: There were very much of those examples, in fact. Every meeting started with allegations about cease-fire violations, and there was a cease-fire ordered from the end of April, so any time this cease-fire was broken, it was, in fact, an order not carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So there were orders coming from whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Orders coming from Mr. Blaskic but also orders signed by General Petkovic, orders signed by General Halilovic, so the top military leaders signed the orders for the cease-fire, the initial orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So then there is not -- you said that the HVO had a very orderly command and the orders were executed, so if they did not execute, sometimes they were not.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Well, not all orders were executed. I think -- if there is a threat at the front-line, then soldiers are likely to answer the fire, so if they can claim that somebody else fired the first shot, then they will answer the fire and fire their weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To a degree, would orders be executed in this situation where there was an eyewitness, for instance, an order not to burn a village. Would it be executed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: It has to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That would be executed. Which orders are you referring to now which might not be executed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: The orders for a total cease-fire. I think they were executed according to artillery, that was well-coordinated and well-controlled by the operational zone level because it was divisional artillery directly controlled by the operational zone commander. The orders to stop all small arms fire, that's more difficult to control that because every soldier that is more or less in panic in his trenches, who feels afraid during the night, he it fire his weapon, and then the cease-fire is broken again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then the higher level --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: On the level of battalions and brigades, maybe on company level, it should be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It should be obeyed.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen? Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel, both sides suffered loss to life, limb, and property; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One side suffered more extensively than another; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's also correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you were there on the ground, and the Tribunal relies on your testimony to guide it. If you were a displaced Croat contemplating the prospect of returning to your home, what would matter to you more? Would a comparison between levels of destruction be decisive in your mind or is it the case that what would weigh with you is the fact that Croat homes and Croat lives were lost?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think the fact that Croat lives were lost would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's turn to another thing. You spoke of intentional exaggerations. By "intentional," I take it that you mean that the Croat leadership knew that the stories which they were putting about were exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, they knew because we reported them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say that that applied also to General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was reported personally, but we reported to his representatives during meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, some of these intentional exaggerations were fed into the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, with what intent do you think that was done?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think the intent was to try to convince the Croat people still living in those certain areas that life was no longer safe for them there and that they should come and unite with the other Croats in Vitez or in Novi Bila or in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If the intent succeeded, could that conceivably affect the configuration of opposing military forces?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think that not only civilians were pulled into the area of Vitez, also the Francopan brigade that used to be stationed in the Zenica area tried to go to Vitez as well, so the forces would come into another balance than before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you're a military man and we're not military people. Tell me: In military academies and schools, do they run courses on the use of disinformation as a method of war?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Sometimes in higher levels, I mean corps or division level, information, so not only disinformation but information itself is being used to sometimes mislead the enemy so it's not used to mislead the civil population but the enemy themselves and certainly not your own population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If you would look at Exhibit -- I think, Mr. Registrar, it is 417C? Would you look at 417C? It is dated 14th June, 1993. Now, would I be correct, Colonel, in my impression that the war went through different phases? During one phase, one side might have the upper hand; during another phase, the advantage may shift?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, on the 14th of June, what was the relative positions of the two opposing forces?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I can only tell by hearsay, Your Honour, because I was on leave during that period of 14th of June, and this document is referring to the Kakanj area, and that was not my area of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you look at a document dated the 8th of June, 1993? And I'm trying to get the exhibit number in a while -- 414, I think, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I have it here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have it? And it is dated the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: At that time, I was in the area of Travnik and Guca Gora, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would you look at the last paragraph at the bottom of page 3 -- shall I read it to you? It says: "The position of the Armija appears strong and morale in the operational group headquarters is high. This contrasts strongly with the HVO operational zone headquarters --" I think that should be "where" "-- where previous arrogance had been replaced by trepidation. The Armija OG commander appeared confident of further gains in the Bila Valley stating he would join UNPROFOR in their HQ for a drink tomorrow and would not require an escort. The ultimate objective of the 3rd Corps is not known but continued advance on the southern access will provide a controlled Travnik-Zenica route." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I see that paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So at that stage, the advantage lay with whom?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's clear, that the Armija forces were winning at that time, and they almost reached their objective for that attack they launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is 8th of June. Do you see any connection between the situation on the 8th of June and the fact that, on the 14th of June, one week later, General Blaskic is putting out a document in the form of 417C in which he's saying that the forces on the other side were, in effect, destroying the Croat people? Do you see any connection?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I can see a connection, Your Honour, but this letter of Mr. Blaskic is based on wrong information. We told him after the 8th of June that it was incorrect, that there was no massacre on the Croat population, that there was no -- or only small damage to Croat property. If he claims that on the same basis of information, then it's wrong, and I think he addressed it on another area, Kakanj and Vares, and that's some 50 kilometres away from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is it your statement to the court that he was erring intentionally?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: If he based his information on the Guca Gora area, then I think he did it intentionally, because we informed him before the 14th that all the allegations concerning the Guca Gora area were untrue. We made that very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, my question to you was intended to ascertain whether there was any connection between his intentionally exaggerating the position in the fact that at around that time, the military advantage lay with the Armija.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I can understand that they have a bad feeling when they're at a disadvantage, of course, but that still, according to my education, my military education, doesn't give you a good reason to mislead your own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand you. Now, could I ask you to look again at Exhibit 417C? It's dated 14th of June. The first line says: "Muslim forces persist in exterminating the Croat people." Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's incorrect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The fourth line from the bottom speaks of massacres.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's also incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The last line says: "On behalf of all the Croats, we beg you to stop the jihad," and it is signed Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, who therefore was speaking on behalf of all the Croats.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think Mr. Blaskic was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, what would you say if you were told that Colonel Blaskic was, at around the same time, telling Muslims, some Muslims, a group of Muslims, that all people should live peacefully together? Do you think so? Do you think he would have been sincere?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us look at Exhibit 422, dated 18th June. It is from Colonel Blaskic; it's a command order. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 8. It refers to POWs, Prisoners of War, does it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Prisoners of War, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And paragraph 9, as you've noticed before, refers to the Geneva Convention and the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: As a military man reading this, you would say that he was telling his soldiers that there could be liability under the laws of war for any transgressions of those laws?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's what he's telling them, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you would say that he was telling his soldiers the laws of war applied?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Look, finally, at Exhibit D148. This is a command order issued by Colonel Blaskic. It's dated 22 April, 1993. Now, look at paragraph 1: "On the territory of the area of responsibility of the Central Bosnia operative zone command controlled by the HVO, I most strictly forbid the torching of houses," et cetera. As a military man reading that, you would say that the writer of this document was asserting military control over the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you also say -- or let me direct you to the part on the top right hand which cites the addressees of the document, and in particular, let me invite your attention to the penultimate line, "Special Purposes Unit, Vitezovi." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then let me direct you to paragraph 2, "The commanders of brigades and independent units must issue this order." Do you see that also?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I see that also, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me invite you to look at paragraph 5: "This order shall take effect immediately, and the commanders of brigades and independent units in the Central Bosnia operative zone are responsible to me for its execution." Would you say that the writer of this document was saying that these independent units, including the Vitezovi unit, were answerable to him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What would you understand to be the meaning of the word "independent" then? Independent of other HVO units but not independent of the commander at the top?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I think in our structure, independent units are units directly under the control of the top level; like, for instance, a communications company, these lines on the bottom of this address list, so not under control of a brigade, as a level in between, but directly under the operational zone command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you one last question. Let me try to relocate you in time and space. You remember your testimony that a military commander of the HVO gave you permission to visit some place, but that on your way to the place, you were stopped, I think, by a single soldier, and he countermanded the order; is that it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct. That was in Gomionica, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The question that was then put to you was whether this suggested that there were two independent lines of authority within the HVO. Do you remember that line of examination?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think you said that that was what you were usually told whenever you got permission and wanted to travel somewhere and you were stopped and you complained to the authorities, they would say something to the same effect, "Well, people down there would do their own thing." Was that --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That was not always the case, but sometimes that was the answer they gave us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes. Now, what was your understanding of the system then? Were there two independent lines of authority, or was it the case that the authority which gave you the licence knew that, in all likelihood, you would be stopped on the way?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That last thing is correct, Your Honour. I think they were just looking for an excuse. They didn't want to debate any longer in the headquarters, so they gave us permission, and on the ground we would be stopped anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you to mean then that all things considered, you are of the view that there was one single line of authority?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have answered many questions, Lieutenant-Colonel. I have only one concern which is still in my mind after what my colleagues have said, and this has to do with the orders. I'm kind of following up on the question that Judge Shahabuddeen, my colleague, asked. I would like to go back to three documents, D147, 148, and 149, all "D." There is actually a fourth one as well. I have put these three together. These are orders in which General Blaskic, who was the commander of the Central Bosnian operative zone, was giving instructions so that the rights of international humanitarian assistance be respected. You haven't been shown these yet, but we're going to show them to you now. The documents, as the registrar has pointed out, have not been admitted as evidence, but we're going to ask you rather general questions anyway. They were not admitted because we did not know about them. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You didn't know about them because they are strictly confidential. One of the questions which the Prosecution asked -- one of the themes, rather, not questions, was to say that the documents demonstrate that Colonel Blaskic admittedly had concerns in respect of the rights of international humanitarian law but that his concerns were not followed up by any execution of things. Nothing was carried out. Do you follow what I'm saying so far?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question that I would like to ask you is that, in an army such as the Dutch army, when this type of order is given, if we were in a war, the sanctions which are taken, should these orders not be carried out, are they published? Are they public? Are they known? Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're asking, Your Honour. I think, because these orders all matter about international law, about violations of humanitarian laws, the Geneva Convention, and all the additional laws, I think that's such an important matter that it's no longer a matter of confidential orders or not. These orders should be discussed openly. It should be clear to everybody, all representatives of the International Community in the area, that the commander in place is doing anything he can to live up to these humanitarian laws, and he didn't -- or they didn't show us anything about that, nothing at all. So there was no sign at all that they issued these orders or that they tried, even tried to live up to the humanitarian laws. So according to the Dutch military system, I think, yes, we should spread out the news that the commander has ordered everybody to live up to the humanitarian laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time of the joint commissions, did General Blaskic or his representatives say to you orally, since the written orders were confidential, that all the measures have been taken in order to have the serious violations of international law stopped?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: Sometimes when an allegation was made, but only sometimes, the answer would be, "Yes, we are taking care of that." But in most cases, the allegation was followed by another contra-allegation, and that went on for hours, so there was no clear reaction on most of the occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'd like you to call upon your memory, and perhaps even your notes, these three documents, D147, 148, and 149, which I said were not admitted as evidence, nonetheless are all part of a very limited time period, the 22nd and 24th of April. The 24th of April -- actually, one says it was at 10.20 in the morning and then at 11.00. Do you remember, short of showing them to you since they're confidential, do you remember having heard this question discussed at all? If you need to, please look at your notes.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: On the 23rd, we have the first meeting of the joint operational command after this order of the 22nd, and this meeting starts again with all kinds of allegations; for instance, stop civilians digging trenches, et cetera, et cetera, release all prisoners. Allegations from both sides; no clear answers to those allegations. On the 24th, we have another meeting, and then I go to Grahovcici for three days, so I was not in the area of Vitez in those three days. Then on the 27th, I go to Kiseljak, and there is then this problem of no entrance into Gomionica and the same allegations again. On the 28th, there is another meeting in Vitez, and it's the same problem. That's a field officer of the UNHCR claiming that people are still being expelled. So I didn't take any notes on positive reactions that HVO would take care of these allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since these documents have not been admitted as evidence, how do you interpret the fact that in the joint commissions, that the representatives of Colonel Blaskic did not say at any point, "But we're making all the arrangements we can. We're making all the steps necessary. Myself or the Colonel has taken all the measures necessary. We can't speak about them to you in any detail, but we did, and we will tell you"? Can you explain why that was not spoken about with the commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK (continued)
utterances.text: That's hard to tell, Your Honour. That's what struck me, when Mr. Hayman showed me these orders, I had never seen them before, and that is the strange thing. We used to discuss all these matters during the joint commission meetings. That's what these commissions were for, to bring trust amongst each other, to bring trust for the International Community, to explain what they did on all these allegations, and there was no positive answer at all. I mean, we were the ones who report to Zagreb and they were the ones who report to Brussels, so what could our politicians do if there was no positive reaction at all? And they didn't give us any positive reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, Colonel Morsink. You agreed to come back; you have been asked many questions. The Tribunal is very grateful to you and now is sending you back to your military activities. We will have you accompanied out of the courtroom and then we will take a break. Have the witness accompanied out of the courtroom, please. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will resume in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor in respect of this afternoon's work, or perhaps tomorrow's as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any additional witnesses this afternoon. We would request, however, that we be permitted to go into closed session to raise an issue with the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will have a closed session now. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Whereupon the court stands adjourned at 4.50 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of July, 1998, at 9.45 a.m

procedural_notes.text: Pages 10100 to 10112 redacted - in closed session
